(CNN) -- President Obama said Tuesday that the country already is "seeing shovels hit the ground" on the first infrastructure repair project funded through the Transportation Department's share of the $787 billion stimulus bill. Workers mark where repairs are needed on Maryland Route 650. Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said, "The work begins today in Montgomery County, Maryland, where a work crew is starting on a project to resurface Maryland State Highway 650 -- a very busy road that has not been fully repaired in 17 years." The resurfacing contract is going to a Pennsylvania-based family-owned company, American Infrastructure, LaHood said. He said the project will support 60 jobs. "And that's how we're going to get the country back on its feet," LaHood added. Mark Compton, director of government affairs for American Infrastructure, said his company received $2.1 million in federal funds, by way of the Maryland State Highway Administration. The money will be used to repave and add safety features to a stretch of the highway. Compton said the cash infusion is the "catalyst" to create 60 jobs, including bringing back some laid-off employees. He said he hopes the workers can be retained beyond this six-month project. "We'll continue to bid, so the goal is to get more projects to keep those guys working, so they can roll off that project onto another," Compton said. CNNMoney: Stimulus funds hit the street . Obama and LaHood on Tuesday announced the release of $27 billion in funds from the stimulus package "to help states create a 21st-century infrastructure." The president said it is part of the "largest new investment in America's infrastructure since President Eisenhower built the Interstate Highway System." Obama said another 200 construction projects would be launched over the next few weeks, "fueling growth in an industry that's been hard hit by our economic crisis." Two weeks ago, Obama signed into law his stimulus plan, known as the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act. The president has said the plan will create or save up to 3.5 million jobs over the next two years. Four-hundred thousand of those will be infrastructure jobs that include rebuilding roads, bridges and schools. LaHood has asked the nation's governors to certify projects and provide assurances that funds from the act will be spent for appropriate infrastructure projects. Obama said transportation projects would be stamped with a special emblem so people can see where their tax dollars are going. Obama said the investments in highways would create or save 150,000 jobs by the end of 2010. The number of jobs being created or saved in one year is more than the number of jobs the Big Three automakers have lost in manufacturing over the past three years, Obama said. By investing in roads "that should have been rebuilt long ago," Obama said, "we can save some 14,000 men and women who lose their lives each year due to bad roads and driving conditions." "Poor roads are a public hazard, and we have a responsibility to fix them," he said.  Watch Obama explain how the roads will save lives » . Obama also announced Tuesday that the Treasury Department and Federal Reserve were launching the Consumer and Business Lending Initiative. When fully implemented, Obama said, the initiative "will generate up to a trillion dollars in new lending for the American people, and this will help unlock our frozen credit markets, which is absolutely essential for economic recovery." CNNMoney's Aaron Smith contributed to this report.

# Obama Announces First Stimulus-Funded Infrastructure Project in Maryland

President Barack Obama and Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood traveled to Maryland on Wednesday to break ground on what officials are calling the first construction project funded through the $787 billion economic stimulus package, marking a symbolic beginning to the administration's ambitious infrastructure spending initiative.

The project, a $2.1 million road resurfacing effort on Maryland State Highway 650, also known as New Hampshire Avenue, has been awarded to American Infrastructure, a Pennsylvania-based construction firm. The relatively modest scope of the project—repaving roughly 6.7 miles of roadway between Washington, D.C., and Baltimore—belies its outsized political and economic significance as the vanguard of a nationwide construction push.

Standing before an audience of construction workers, local officials, and members of his economic team, Obama emphasized both the immediate and long-term benefits of the spending.

"This is just the beginning," Obama said. "We're not going to rest until every road, every bridge, every piece of critical infrastructure that needs repair gets the attention it deserves, and until every American who wants to work has the chance to do so."

Officials estimate the Maryland project alone will support approximately 60 jobs, encompassing everything from equipment operators and laborers to project managers and suppliers. While modest in scale compared to the overall stimulus package, the administration has framed the project as proof that stimulus dollars are translating into real jobs and tangible infrastructure improvements.

LaHood, a former Republican congressman tapped by Obama to lead the Transportation Department, used the occasion to outline the broader scope of the department's stimulus allocation. According to LaHood, the Maryland project represents just the first trickle of what will become a flood of infrastructure spending, with $27 billion in Transportation Department stimulus funds set to be distributed for projects across the country.

"This is only the start," LaHood told reporters. "In the coming weeks, we expect roughly 200 additional construction projects to break ground in states from coast to coast. Every one of these projects means jobs—jobs for construction workers, jobs for engineers, jobs for the people who supply the materials that make these projects possible."

The administration has repeatedly emphasized the historic scale of the infrastructure investment contained within the stimulus package. Obama, in remarks echoing statements he has made in previous speeches on the topic, described the effort as the most significant investment in American infrastructure since President Dwight D. Eisenhower's construction of the interstate highway system in the 1950s.

"Just as President Eisenhower recognized that America needed a modern highway system to grow our economy and connect our country, we recognize that rebuilding our infrastructure today is essential to our economic recovery and our long-term competitiveness," Obama said.

The stimulus package, formally known as the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, was signed into law by Obama in February amid the depths of the financial crisis and mounting job losses. The legislation allocated tens of billions of dollars toward transportation infrastructure, including highways, bridges, transit systems, and rail projects, as part of a broader strategy to jumpstart economic activity while addressing long-neglected infrastructure needs.

Critics of the stimulus package have questioned both the pace of spending and its overall effectiveness in creating jobs, with some Republican lawmakers arguing that infrastructure projects take too long to plan and execute to provide the rapid economic boost the administration promised. Administration officials have pushed back against these criticisms, arguing that shovel-ready projects like the Maryland resurfacing effort demonstrate that stimulus funds can be deployed quickly and efficiently.

Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley, who joined Obama and LaHood at the event, praised the project as an example of federal and state cooperation in addressing infrastructure needs that predate the economic crisis.

"Maryland, like states across the country, has infrastructure needs that have been deferred for too long," O'Malley said. "This funding allows us to address those needs while putting people to work at a time when they desperately need jobs."

As the ceremonial first shovels went into the ground along Highway 650, administration officials expressed confidence that the pace of project announcements would accelerate significantly in the weeks ahead, with the 200 additional projects expected to encompass a wide range of transportation infrastructure work across multiple states.

The White House has indicated that it will continue to highlight individual infrastructure projects funded by the stimulus as a way of demonstrating tangible progress to a public increasingly anxious about the pace of economic recovery and the effectiveness of the massive spending package.

# Obama Announces First Stimulus-Funded Infrastructure Project on Maryland Highway

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — President Obama traveled to Maryland on Wednesday to break ground on the first infrastructure project funded by the $787 billion economic stimulus package, marking a milestone in the administration's effort to jumpstart the sluggish economy through public works spending.

The president visited a stretch of Maryland Route 650, also known as New Hampshire Avenue, in Prince George's County, where crews will begin repaving and rehabilitating a roughly two-mile section of the busy commuter corridor connecting Washington's northern suburbs.

"This is only the beginning," Obama said at the site, flanked by construction workers in hard hats and orange vests. "In the coming weeks and months, we're going to see roads and bridges rebuilt all across America, and we're going to see people going back to work."

The Route 650 project, valued at approximately $2.4 million, will fund repaving, drainage improvements, and safety upgrades along the heavily traveled route, which serves thousands of commuters daily between Maryland and the District of Columbia. State officials said the project would employ dozens of local workers within weeks and serve as a model for how stimulus dollars would move quickly into communities.

Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood, who joined the president at the event, said the project exemplified the kind of "shovel-ready" work the administration has emphasized in distributing stimulus funds.

"This is what the Recovery Act is all about — putting people back to work rebuilding America's infrastructure," LaHood said. "We're not talking about projects that are years away. We're talking about work that starts now, that puts people in these communities back on the job now."

LaHood added that the Department of Transportation was working to expedite funding to states so that similar projects could break ground across the country in the coming weeks. "Maryland moved fast, and they should be commended for that," he said. "We want to see that same urgency everywhere."

The stimulus package, signed into law by Obama last month, includes roughly $48 billion for transportation infrastructure, with billions more directed toward broader public works, energy, and construction projects. Administration officials have faced pressure to demonstrate quickly that the massive spending bill is translating into real jobs, especially as unemployment continues to climb nationally.

Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley, who also attended the event, praised the speed with which the state was able to secure funding. "We were ready to go, and now Marylanders are going to see the benefits of this investment sooner rather than later," O'Malley said.

Critics of the stimulus package have questioned whether relatively small projects like the Route 650 repaving will have a meaningful impact on the broader economy, and Republican lawmakers have continued to raise concerns about the bill's overall cost and effectiveness.

But Obama used the appearance to push back against skeptics, arguing that projects across the country — even modest ones — would add up to a substantial economic boost. "It may not seem like a lot to some folks, but for the workers who get to go to work tomorrow because of this project, it makes all the difference," he said.

The White House said additional infrastructure projects funded by the stimulus are expected to be announced in the coming days as more states finalize plans to put Recovery Act dollars to use.

# Obama Administration Stimulus: Transportation Infrastructure & Lending Initiative

## Transportation Infrastructure Rollout

The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA), signed in February 2009, included significant funding for transportation infrastructure as part of its broader economic recovery goals. Key elements included:

- **Highway and road projects**: Billions allocated for repairing and building roads, bridges, and highways across states
- **Public transit investments**: Funding for buses, rail systems, and transit infrastructure upgrades
- **"Shovel-ready" emphasis**: The administration prioritized projects that could begin quickly to generate immediate employment
- **State-by-state distribution**: Funds were distributed through formulas to state departments of transportation

## Job Creation Figures

The administration cited various job creation/preservation estimates tied to infrastructure spending, though these figures were often contested:

- Officials frequently cited economic models suggesting billions in infrastructure spending would create or save hundreds of thousands of jobs
- The Council of Economic Advisers periodically released reports estimating jobs "created or saved" by ARRA overall, including construction and transportation sectors
- Critics and some economists questioned the methodology behind these estimates, noting difficulty in isolating stimulus effects from natural economic recovery

## Consumer and Business Lending Initiative

This initiative, announced in March 2009, aimed to address credit market freezes by:

- **Expanding TALF** (Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility) to unfreeze markets for consumer and small business loans
- **Supporting auto and student loans**, credit card lending, and small business lending by purchasing asset-backed securities
- **Treasury and Federal Reserve coordination** to inject liquidity into secondary markets for loans

---

If you need specific figures (exact dollar amounts, precise job numbers, or particular program names), I'd recommend verifying against Recovery.gov archives, GAO reports, or Treasury Department historical records, as I may be conflating details or lack full precision on this topic.

Officials pointed to specific corridors — including sections of interstate highways in the Midwest and Southeast — where resurfacing and improved lighting have already coincided with double-digit percentage drops in accident reports over the past year.

"When you fix a pothole, you're not just saving someone's shocks and struts," said one Transportation Department official traveling with the president. "You're potentially saving a life."

**Political Backdrop**

The announcement arrives amid continued congressional debate over the scale and pace of infrastructure spending, with critics questioning the long-term cost-effectiveness of stimulus-funded projects. Republican lawmakers have argued that while road repairs offer visible, short-term benefits, the administration should present a clearer plan for sustained infrastructure funding beyond the initial stimulus package.

The White House, for its part, has framed the road projects as a down payment on a broader vision — one that pairs immediate job creation with long-term investment in America's aging infrastructure.

Obama, addressing the criticism directly, said: "This is just the beginning. We didn't get into this hole overnight, and we're not going to build our way out overnight either. But this is what progress looks like — mile by mile, job by job."
